references.text: In [ref:Matt 24:32-33|Matthew 24:32-33], Jesus gives the same parable about the fig tree: "Learn this lesson from the fig tree: When its branch becomes tender and puts forth leaves, you know that summer is near." This is the parallel passage in Matthew's Gospel.

[ref:Mark 13:28-29|Mark 13:28-29] is the synoptic parallel where Jesus uses the fig tree as a parable to show that signs in nature point toward what is coming, just as end-time signs point toward the coming of the Son of Man.

In [ref:Luk 13:6-9|Luke 13:6-9], Jesus tells the parable of the fig tree that bore no fruit. The fig tree is also used there as a symbol with spiritual meaning, which thematically connects it to its use as an image in Luke 21:29.

[ref:Jak 5:7-8|James 5:7-8] speaks of the farmer waiting patiently for the precious fruit of the earth and urges patience because the Lord's coming is near. The parable about trees putting forth buds carries a similar thought: natural signs show that the time is drawing near.

In [ref:Høys 2:11-13|Song of Solomon 2:11-13], it describes how winter has passed, the fig tree ripens its fruit, and the vine blossoms – nature's signs that a new season is breaking forth. Jesus uses a similar natural image in his parable about the fig tree.

In [ref:Joel 1:7|Joel 1:7], the fig tree is mentioned as being laid waste. The fig tree is a recurring symbol in the Old Testament for Israel's condition, and this adds depth to Jesus' use of the fig tree as a sign in his end-time discourse.

In [ref:Matt 21:19-21|Matthew 21:19-21], Jesus curses the fig tree that bears no fruit, and it withers. Here the fig tree is used as a powerful symbolic image, forming the background for its further use as an image in Jesus' teaching.
